The annual Fleece Amateur Shrub Trimming Contest went ahead as scheduled, but this year something astonishing happened. For a rookie reporter like me, a scoop falling out of the sky like this was a true godsend, and I bounded to the scene like a Followg leaping at bait.
Mr. Palm, from the Rosia Empire, entered at a friend's invitation and won with his piece "The Perfect Square," earning the highest score in contest history. But at what should have been a moment of celebration, right after accepting the prize, he charged at the second-place entry with garden shears in hand. In just three snips, the runner-up piece "Dancing Chimomo" became "Smooth Xiaoyu": every branch lopped off, the shrub left a perfect sphere.
As a result, Mr. Palm was stripped of his eligibility and his title for deliberately vandalizing another contestant's work.
Asked about his motive afterward, he admitted he's actually a bit high-strung...
"A friend talked me into entering. Said, 'Trim that thing into a square and you'll make some Uni.' It wasn't hard, so I finished quickly, but what the person next to me cut... I just couldn't stand it. Don't those extra branches bother you? Ugh, I was so uncomfortable I couldn't stop breaking out in a cold sweat..."
"Shut up!"
Mid-interview, the creator of "Dancing Chimomo" came running over.
"That's a Chimomo, not a Xiaoyu! And those branches weren't extra! They're an abstract rendering of Chimomo's tentacles!"
The heated argument turned the heads of the other contestants and spectators one after another. Oops, looks like another fistfight has broken out. At this rate I won't be short of material for the next issue.
In any case, the title went to the de facto third place: Paul, a boy living in Fleece. His piece, titled "Burning Art," was highly original, made not with garden shears but by trimming the shrub with fire. The scorch marks dotting the lush green shrub are scars where the plant was torn by flame, and the remaining branches and leaves reaching upward with those scars show an indomitable vitality that left a powerful impression on viewers. This piece is truly the most concrete expression of the pain of growing up.
